Ultimately, this research concentrates on the first approach and surveys the existing DP graph analytics studies in detail, summarizing key points based on data models and DP mechanisms used. It's the author's intention to provide a foundational framework for future work in DP graph analytics.

The vast amount of images, data, and resources that Euclid will generate positions the consortium to assemble comprehensive legacy databases of all its data, ensuring long-term accessibility for researchers across the globe. These databases will encompass not only processed datasets but also raw data, enabling high-quality imaging and extensive spectroscopy to significantly advance our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution.

In this research, we propose a method for automatically generating complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. We utilize a control point approach to create and modify a dynamic road layout that responds to the agent's actions. By systematically adjusting these control points, we can efficiently test lane-keeping performance in a controlled environment. A key aspect of our method is its ability to decouple control point manipulation from simulation physics, preventing unrealistic scenarios such as road bridges suddenly appearing. We developed two ways to automatically adjust control points for predefined durations and found that our method can produce diverse and predictable geometry outcomes. Furthermore, our approach yields more varied scenarios compared to commonly used models.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach within the positive-P phase-space formalism. This method is particularly effective for systems of interacting Bose gases, and we've demonstrated its value by simulating a far-from-equilibrium scenario, namely the $T$-damping situation, where a coherent state decays into thermal fluctuations. Comparing our results to both exact simulations and Ginzburg-Landau-Feynman path integrals, we found that the T-damping dynamics can be accurately captured, including a precise balance between coherent and thermal components, as well as a precise description of the associated power spectrum.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in the vast variety of action types and locations present in videos. Existing methods often struggle to effectively identify and integrate different parts of an action. In this work, we introduce a new network, named Boundary-aware Relation Network (BRR), that addresses this issue by integrating the boundaries of the action with internal parts relations. BRR initially estimates the action boundaries using a proposed boundary branch, which is then used to refine the fusion of parts inside the action region through a relation branch. Notably, we do not require manual annotation of action boundaries during training or testing. Our method achieves impressive results on two major benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in temporal action detection. The code for BRR is freely available at https://github.com/HarryGuo2015/BRR.

Space-compact entities in plasma turbulence, often called current vortices or flux tubes, are flux surfaces that exist apart from the average and carry parallel currents.  In the presence of significant parallel currents, the ideal MHD equations can be represented by a magnetic map in the form of $\vec{B} = 
abla \psi 	imes 
abell{e}_\ell + 
abell{e}_\ell I(\psi)$, where $\psi$ maps out surfaces parallel to the magnetic field lines and $\ell$ is the coordinate along the direction of the largest system. A new approach is presented to study the statistical characteristics of current vortices in a range of scenarios, utilizing the magnetic helicity and a quasinormal mode analysis of the $\psi$ function. The current vortices identified through this approach exhibit properties consistent with those of the current vortices in solar coronal loops and demonstrate the ability to merge, splitting the magnetic field lines within the vortices. The approach also provides a basis for deriving an equation to describe the evolution of the $\psi$ function, which can be utilized to investigate the properties of current vortices in more complex, three-dimensional scenarios.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields that change based on the robots' velocities. A simplified model of interacting robots in a 2-D plane is developed, accompanied by an analysis of the equilibrium and transient behavior of potential fields, as well as proofs of the absence of virtual singularities and unbounded growth in the robot-obstacle system. We propose a velocity-based approach to collision avoidance, and our theoretical findings suggest that the constant speed forward motion of robots can be maintained while avoiding virtual singularities and unbounded growth in the system.

Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters from an arbitrary source with a fixed entropy, the annealed large deviation principle was established for a system that encodes a sequence of messages without a fixed entropy. The system's behavior is governed by a rate function derived from a combination of specific relative entropy and a weighted sum of probabilities. The principle is not valid for source entropies that exceed a certain threshold, where a different kind of relative entropy becomes relevant. Additionally, the system's source error exponent was defined and a sudden shift in the value of this exponent was observed, marking a significant change in the rate function's behavior. The system also exhibits a form of equivocation where the relative entropy between the original distribution and the behavior of a typical sequence with a specific source entropy remains constant, regardless of the source entropy. Finally, a direct application of this principle was used to confirm the accuracy of a previously conjectured form of the source error exponent.

Recent advancements in wireless communications and radar have introduced intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) to improve target parameter estimation and signal reception. This paper investigates a novel application of IRS in radar, where the surface is designed to directly enhance the radar return signal from the target. This approach offers distinct advantages over conventional passive reflecting surfaces, providing greater control over the radar signal and potential improvements in estimation accuracy. A closed-form expression for the range-Doppler spectrum is derived, enabling optimal target parameter estimation. Furthermore, a comparison with existing IRS-assisted radar schemes is provided, and simulation results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed scheme in target parameter estimation.

Automated mutation analysis evaluates the effectiveness of tests in identifying program bugs.
The evaluation involves determining the rate of mutations a program's test suite can detect.
Calculating this rate requires the creation of a multitude of mutations.
However, the creation of these mutations is often a labor-intensive process that demands human intervention.
We present an approach that automates the creation of mutations for programs written in Java.
Our method utilizes abstract syntax trees and byte-based mutations to produce a consistent set of mutations for Java programs.
These mutations are produced in the form of instrumented Java code, allowing for integration with existing measurement tools.
Our approach is demonstrated through the integration of mutations with CodeCoverage in an Apache Maven-based project.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves. Using this definition, we can construct relatively 1-homomorphic mappings with minimized energy within a given 1-homotopy class for the spaces in question. A key finding of our research is that local smoothness can be guaranteed for certain types of mappings when the target space has a limited number of singularities. Additionally, we establish a local smoothness property for mappings that minimize a specific measure of complexity between a higher-genre surface and a limitation on a disk-shaped area.

This study provides evidence of the quasiconvergence of solutions to semilinear parabolic equations defined on the closure of an open bounded domain in R^n, given suitable regularity conditions on the function f. Specifically, under these conditions, solutions exhibit a stable behavior where differences between solution trajectories at any two points decay exponentially when normalized by the corresponding local means. This result is particularly significant as it does not require conditions on the source term f. Additionally, we derive a corollary demonstrating the quasiconvergence of trajectories when f is continuous. Furthermore, we also obtain the quasirelaxation of functionals associated with the equation when the source term is not necessarily continuous.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus have uncovered several highly excited states, 
including some with significant energy. Using a combined approach of shell model and 
collective rotation, we determined the rotational characteristics of a few of these 
excited states. Our analysis revealed the rotational nature of some previously 
unidentified 4+ states at energies between 4500 keV and 5360 keV, which were confirmed 
through a combination of theoretical calculations and experimental data.

We develop a specific probability ratio of a game's Lipschitz continuity to its uniform stability, and show that in this ratio being bounded, randomized algorithms can efficiently find nearly optimal equilibria in a specific range of game types, including those where strategies are continuous and bounded, and another group where strategy sets are defined by simple constraints and there is a certain degree of smoothness in the function describing a player's outcome based on the strategies of others. Achieving this efficiency is done through a specific algorithm, and we establish its convergence to a specific equilibrium through a similar ratio, and establish a limitation to finding a specific group of equilibrium through a specific probability ratio, and show that a specific group of games can efficiently find a certain group of equilibrium through a specific ratio, and show that a specific algorithm for a specific group of games with a certain degree of smoothness can find a certain group of equilibria through a similar ratio, and show that a specific algorithm for a specific group of games with a certain degree of smoothness can find a certain group of equilibria through a similar ratio, and show that a specific algorithm for a specific group of games with a certain degree of smoothness can find a certain group of equilibria through a similar ratio.

Machine learning model development involves a model's parameter configuration using cross-validation and a performance evaluation via validation datasets. The optimal configuration is selected based on best validation performance. Due to high computational costs of training deep learning models multiple times, the number of feasible configuration options is limited. Unfortunately, limited configuration search can lead to suboptimal performance in real-world applications. To address this issue, we propose an efficient method for effective hyperparameter optimization using iterative Bayesian inference, reducing the need for full model retraining during configuration search. Our method uses a Bayesian framework to infer optimal configuration by iteratively updating a Bayesian network with validation performance data. We demonstrate our method's superior performance on various language modeling and image classification models compared to traditional CVA, using a smaller configuration search cost.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved great success in computer vision, but their application is often limited by expensive labeling costs. To overcome this, researchers have explored using Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge learning. These architectures utilize a Teacher network to guide a Student network in learning from limited labels. Due to their success, they have various applications, including compact model design, large model pruning, and semi-supervised learning.

However, the effectiveness of the Teacher-Student architecture relies heavily on the quality of knowledge transferred from the Teacher network. Unfortunately, traditional methods of generating the Teacher labels, such as hard target replacement, are hindered by error propagation. To address this issue, we propose Co-Knowledge Distillation, a novel framework that simultaneously optimizes the Student network and the Teacher labels. This is achieved by formulating a joint optimization problem that considers both the Student network and the Teacher labels. By deriving a closed-form solution, we can update the Teacher labels and the Student network in a more efficient manner. Co-Knowledge Distillation enables the exploration of soft targets with a smaller entropy, resulting in more accurate predictions and a reduced error propagation. Our approach outperforms existing methods on multiple benchmarks and provides a solid foundation for further research in knowledge learning.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework to develop an effective approximate inference technique using deterministic finite state automata. Additionally, we demonstrate that our framework can be used to create a compact history-tipping variant of particle filters capable of handling sequences of observations.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. The absorption pattern deviates from the expected shape due to changes in the frequency of the remaining photons after interacting with multiple atoms, which also affects how those atoms move. In contrast to earlier studies that examined only a couple of absorption events or didn't consider the movement of the atoms, our work analyzes an infinite number of absorptions and scattering events, taking into account the motion of the atoms. Additionally, our model can be applied to other situations involving slow-absorbers and can be used to study the effects of recoil on the absorption of fast-absorbing light. The absorption pattern observed in our experiment matches our predictions very closely. The discrepancy between the experiment and theory is likely caused by a factor in the experiment that allows absorption at two different frequencies. Our findings have significant implications for precision measurements involving lasers at specific atomic transitions.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden transformation, transforming from stable states to rapidly flowing states. This transformation involves a significant increase in viscosity and can cause material failure. Understanding this phenomenon is crucial in addressing long-standing questions about dense mixtures' intrinsic stability and the role of material defects in this context. Using a novel approach that combines molecular dynamics simulations with a coarse-grained model featuring attractive forces, our research has developed a comprehensive numerical framework to analyze the dynamics of stress-induced failure. This computational model has been applied to study model systems, and our findings have been validated against experimental data and previous studies. For systems governed by repulsive forces, we have identified the coexistence of high-stress and low-stress states as well as first-order phase separation. For systems governed by attractive forces, we have observed phase separation as well as phase coexistence with a low-stress state. In our analysis of systems governed by attractive forces, we have observed that the interaction dynamics change significantly during the failure transition, and this transformation can be mapped to a phase diagram. Our findings have been used to explain the dynamics of phase separation and stress-induced failure in two-dimensional systems governed by attractive forces.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a byproduct. We establish that $sR(n)$ is closely linked to the centralizer $Z_{n-1}$ of the embedding of $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ into itself in a specific way, and demonstrate that $Z_{n-1}$ is actually equal to a direct sum of $sR(k)$ for various $k$. This relationship is derived using the Gelfand-Tsetlin basis, and we also provide the special case of $sR(4)$ with explicit basis elements.

Our study examines how quantum phase transitions in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice are affected by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, particularly in a large-magnon regime. Using a Gutzwiller variational approach, we analyze the system's accuracy and find that its competitive interactions can drive a transition from an ordered state to superfluid and supersolid phases at a specific threshold. This threshold is dependent on the magnetic polarization, interlayer and intralayer interactions but is independent of the DDM. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the DM interaction determines the magnetic structure of the superfluid and supersolid phases. Calculated quantities, such as interlayer magnetization densities and magnetic densities within and between layers, provide evidence that the system is accurately described by the quantum phase model. Consequently, we identify a relatively low energy necessary for achieving twisted supersfluid and supersolid phases, specifically around -0.16J when the DDM is set to 2J.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our findings suggest that incorporating angular dependence into existing calculations can significantly alter the estimated number of successful scatterings within that specific energy range, particularly for gold targets at both low and high energy levels, and for oxygen targets. Given the relatively large angular spread of future experiments like DARWIN and LEGEND, the inclusion of angular dependence may have a substantial impact on their sensitivity to WIMPs, especially in the lower mass range.

An emerging trend of Web search personalisation is gaining popularity. While it can tailor search results to a user's needs, it also raises significant privacy concerns. Our investigation of existing research on the topic reveals that Web search personalisation is not always beneficial and may overestimate its positive impact. In some cases, up to 40% of crucial information could be excluded from search results due to personalised settings being turned off. To explore this issue further, we undertook a series of experiments involving 100 Google users who performed real-world tasks on both non-personalised and personalised search engines. Our findings show that Web search personalisation can lead to the exclusion of relevant information from up to 20% of users' top 10 search results. Furthermore, we discovered that users who used a non-personalised search engine were better able to identify sensitive information that was inadvertently included in personalised search results. Our research also uncovered that Web search personalisation often results in a one-size-fits-all approach, where the same results are recommended to all users, thereby undermining its purported privacy benefits. Overall, our findings suggest that Web search personalisation can have a range of unintended consequences, from compromising users' privacy to excluding relevant information from search results.

We suggest establishing a next-generation collider based on high-intensity, low-emipation muon beams and a compact, cost-effective muon accelerator. Such a facility, utilizing 100 and 15000 GeU muon beams, could transform research in particle and nuclear physics through muon-proton, muon-nucleus, and even muon-muon collisions. The sACLA design concept, a streamlined accelerator for accelerating and focusing these beams, is also outlined.

A novel approach is proposed to create a respiratory-synchronized 4D MRI dataset from a standard 3D MRI scan. This novel approach leverages an adaptive sparse coding method, an enhanced dictionary learning algorithm, a respiratory motion model, and a maximum a posteriori estimation step. This method is capable of generating a 4D MRI dataset by reconstructing multiple 3D volumes from SPIRAL k-t data sampled at different time points during each spiral scan. An experiment was conducted to test this method using a phantom, and the results showed that it can accurately recover a 4D MRI dataset, even in the presence of missing k-t data points. An improvement in signal-to-noise ratio was observed when comparing it to linear interpolation, and the standard 4D MRI acquisition method served as a comparison in this study.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate capability in handling system input constraints. To illustrate its effectiveness, the paper includes both a theoretical convergence proof and a practical application in robotics.

In this work, approximation spaces are classified using rough set theory based on the CF-matrix, which is shown to be equivalent to a specific category of approximations under CF-relations. These relations are further analyzed in terms of their properties, with notable examples being preorder and partial order relations. CF-quotients are defined based on partial order relations, with applications to the identification of common structures, such as lattices and moore families. Notable findings include the identification of a basic lattice structure in CF-quotients and a generation property for CF-quotients. Additionally, a connection is established between moore family quotients and the intersection of moore family approximations.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. However, this test's effectiveness can be compromised by a lack of sufficient sample size due to the computational cost of a single evaluation. This issue is further exacerbated in NLP systems with high cost per evaluation, causing confidence intervals to widen significantly. To address this concern, an experiment was conducted to assess the test's reliability, which indicated that at least 30 data points are needed for accurate results. To overcome these limitations, an innovative approach was proposed - a fast approximation test of paired-permutation test based on mini-batch estimation. This approach utilizes a single evaluation to generate coupled predictions for multiple test instances within a batch, which can be predicted concurrently. This method significantly reduces the computational cost of a paired-permutation test, making it feasible for high-cost NLP systems. An in-depth analysis was performed to assess the performance of the proposed approach, which indicated that a mini-batch size of 50 is optimal for most NLP tasks. This results in a 5 times reduction in computational cost compared to a traditional paired-permutation test, with only a slight decrease in accuracy (around 1%) of the full test.

A comprehensive dataset has been assembled, encompassing a vast array of data points related to standard and non-standard shipping container prices from 1980 to 2016.

To investigate the 2005-2016 container market anomaly, an econometric analysis was performed on the dataset.

The primary determinants that drove the emergence of the container crisis were found to be an unbalanced market, characterized by the high cost of container returns, combined with surging global trade.

Furthermore, container leasing and a subsequent supply surge following the introduction of rental pricing guidelines were also key factors contributing to the crisis.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, implying that the realization of the link space as a polyhedral structure from piecewise linear geometry.

Graph neural networks have shown significant potential in various applications.  However, their increasing complexity poses challenges, particularly in terms of interpretability.  To address this issue, we introduce the Kedge method, a novel approach that maintains model accuracy while reducing the number of graph connections.  Unlike traditional methods that rely on thresholding or sub-neural network operations to prune the graph, Kedge applies a single, learnable operation to the graph's edge weights.  Our method is efficient, requiring only one extra multiplication per original operation, and can be used with any graph neural network architecture.  Experimental results on multiple graph neural network models and datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Kedge in significantly reducing the number of graph connections while maintaining model performance.  Notably, Kedge achieved a 9.6-fold reduction in the number of edges while achieving parity with the original model accuracy on the Cora dataset when used with Graph Neural Network.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (such as maximum values) of a vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in scenarios where the identified top elements need to be retrieved in a specific order corresponding to their associated values. A more suitable approach, DropCountSketch, has been proposed to replace CountSketch for this ordered identification purpose. The utility of DRS in various applications, including identifying heavy hitters and ranking estimation, has been shown to rely on the ability to identify top elements in order, thereby benefiting from the use of DropCountSketch. Analytical proofs have been provided to evaluate the performance of the DRS in terms of identifying correct elements along with their order. Moreover, drop-in influence has been analytically proved to play a crucial role in the DRS performance. The study also provides optimal guidance on controlling the probability of drop-in occurrences.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ an area expansion method from Daniel Farber and the author to establish an  n -dimensional minimal obstacle theory, ultimately using it to prove the existence of infinitely many singular minimal geometries with distinct areas.

rotating the sample around its axis, while maintaining a longitudinal thermal

where H is the applied magnetic field strength. This effect, occurring in a

response and measurements of the Hall voltage across rotating samples at
different rates of rotation, in the presence of H parallel to the samples'
c-axis, will provide a direct way of determining the friction coefficient of

Effective management of complex systems with multiple inputs and outputs is crucial in modern engineering. We have developed a novel control strategy, called penalized predictive control (PPC), based on an alternative formulation of the optimized tail problem (OTP) in time series analysis. Unlike the OTP, the PPC takes into account current and forecasted errors while minimizing a penalized term for control input changes. The advantages of the PPC method over conventional model predictive control (MPC) are highlighted through theoretical analysis and a practical case study on the NASA Space Shuttle's fuel tank pressurization system. The PPC method's benefits are demonstrated by the system's improved stability and response time.

The recent advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly in natural language processing, have been hindered by a lack of freely available, high-quality datasets. This paper introduces a novel, large-scale dataset comprising over 1.2 million entries. It consists of paired pairs of YouTube video captions and corresponding stock market data, centered around popular companies mentioned in online videos. This unique resource can facilitate the exploration of connections between media coverage and its impact on the value of mentioned companies. Our accompanying analysis provides valuable insights into the structure of the data and its potential applications.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where the inner component is thought to emit gravitational waves, yet confirming this is challenging. We have developed a comprehensive model of CE evolution, incorporating the effects of spiral-in, plunging, and merger, and derived an equation for the CE's apparent size. We applied our model to specific cases of plunging and spiral-in endings, and found that the spiral-in's long GW signal is typically overshadowed by the CE's envelope. Additionally, our findings suggest that observations of massive black hole mergers may provide the best chance of directly detecting gravitational waves generated during the CE phase.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future high-energy colliders, specifically the 100 TeV FCC-hh and the 500 GeV CLIC, within the framework of Effective Field Theory (EFT). Initially, we establish a precise threshold for when the validity of the EFT description is compromised due to the introduction of new physics at scale Λ. Subsequently, we calculate the single and double Higgs boson production cross-sections, taking into account the single and double Higgs precursors. Our analysis initially considers a simplified 'Type-I' EFT extension of the Standard Model, and we derive corrections to the relevant quartic scalar couplings based on the decay properties of the Higgs boson. We then assess the implications of these findings for cross-sectional predictions at future colliders, considering different values of Λ. The results indicate that in Type-I, the dominant new physics contributions to single and double Higgs boson production originate from dimension-8 operators. Moreover, we determine a critical Λ threshold beyond which the double Higgs component significantly surpasses the single Higgs component. The implications of this threshold on the cross-section to the number of observed Higgs bosons are also explored. The results obtained in the context of the Effective Field Theory are then contrasted with a more comprehensive calculation that incorporates both single and double Higgs precursors within a specific Beyond Standard Model theory, in this case, a two-Higgs Doublet Model with a specific

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed of
light. We achieve this through an appropriate rescaling of spatial derivatives,
without relying on any further assumptions about spacetime structure, such as
Newton-Cartan geometry. This method yields an generalization of the ADM
decomposition within the Einstein gravity framework. It also provides an
interpretation of the momentum conjugate to the metric's time derivative and
contributes to understanding the Hamiltonian constraint in Einstein gravity.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, by simplifying the complex Einstein equations. It is demonstrated that using a first-order approximation yields highly accurate results, which can be iteratively refined to obtain exact solutions. The method is user-friendly and efficient, as it allows for the direct comparison of its outputs with those of the full, non-linear equations. The framework is applied to study the shock's long-term behavior, including the formation of stable waves that decay over time, as well as the conditions under which these waves can be eliminated to achieve a flat, stationary state.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polystyrene and silica grains, at various speeds and orientations. The cylinder's axis was aligned either parallel or perpendicular to the direction of motion, and we found the drag force's anisotropy to be significantly influenced by the intruder's length-to-diameter ratio, the material's properties, and the speed of motion. Furthermore, we discovered that the anisotropy of drag becomes less pronounced as the speed of motion increases, eventually converging to a common value at high speeds, indicating a transition regime where the drag experienced is largely independent of orientation. This transition occurs at different speed thresholds depending on the density of the grains, and we observed this phenomenon to occur around ten times the intruder's diameter. We also found that in regions of sparse grain flow, the anisotropy of drag converges to a ratio of approximately 1.33, a value previously unreported in the literature.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows relate to the galaxy's properties. Our analysis shows a strong correlation, with outflow mass flux directly related to the rate of gas being converted into stars per unit area. We also found evidence of a mass outflow efficiency greater than one, indicating that more mass is ejected from the galaxy than the mass locked up in newly formed stars and gas. Furthermore, our study highlights the impact of outflows on the momentum and mass outflows in the galaxy, with a distinct break in these outflows at a specific threshold of the SFR surface density.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to the massive number of possible configurations, which can lead to significant performance variations. These frameworks typically rely on Bayesian models to generalize from sampled configurations, but they often fail to capture the underlying structure of the configuration space. As a result, the associated costs of exploration and exploitation become difficult to quantify. We propose Structured Bayesian Optimization, an adaptive active learning approach that leverages the intrinsic structure of the problem to efficiently identify low-latency network configurations in computer systems. By applying this method to the FatTree network topology, our experiments demonstrate that structured optimization outperforms traditional approaches in terms of precision and recall at the 5th best solution, while also reducing the sampling requirements by up to 50%. We have made our code and datasets publicly available at https://github.com/structuredbo/fattree.

Our analysis of the ANNA v. 3.0 code for ANNs reveals that the flow parameter $v_3$ exhibits a clear dependence on collision centrality, contrary to previous findings with the default configuration. A centrically symmetric peak in $v_3$ versus $v_3$ plots indicates the need for $v_3$ in flow parameter studies. Utilizing generated data that replicates experimental conditions, our research identifies three key factors in the code's architecture that can restore the expected $v_3$ pattern. These components are independently modular and can be integrated into existing ANN models.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has significantly increased, but unfortunately, many datasets suffer from poor quality issues. Data management tasks are further complicated by varied data formats and linked data characteristics. Our research focuses on linked data cleaning, specifically the detection of inconsistencies in property values. We've developed an innovative approach to identifying duplicate entities across datasets, which involves a scoring system based on entity pair extraction and ranking. Our proposed method uses a linear classifier to efficiently extract a small set of relevant entity pairs from large datasets, resulting in improved performance and cost-effectiveness.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed to facilitate subsequent statistical analysis, such as calculating reliable confidence intervals or performing hypothesis tests. However, using maximum likelihood estimation for these purposes can lead to biased results and inaccurate confidence estimates, especially in cases of small sample sizes. To address this issue, a confidence region based on a tilting method was developed for independent and identically distributed data, and the resulting bounds provide a more accurate assessment of parameter uncertainty. Although this method may not always be optimally efficient, its robustness and reliability make it valuable when working with limited data. The proposed confidence region can also serve as a starting point for further refinement through optimization methods in cases of small samples.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within the central regions of three bright Seyfert galaxies, specifically MCG +01-13-015, Mrk 7138, and Mrk 7177. By analyzing their X-ray spectra using the aevm model, we discovered that electron temperatures varied significantly, primarily due to differences in ionization levels. Our results show a correlation between temperature and oxygen ionization state, with higher ions indicating lower electron temperatures. This variation can be explained through radiative recombination and Coulomb collisions, with the ionization structure likely shaped by an ionizing photon spectrum and the gas distribution. Furthermore, our data suggest a connection between soft X-ray spectral features and the electron temperature, particularly the ionization of softer X-ray lines like O VII.

As IoT systems grow in complexity, ensuring the reliability and security of IoT applications becomes increasingly difficult for software testers due to the vast number of possible hardware configurations and the limited testing options available to software suppliers who cannot test their software on different devices. To address this challenge, we present an innovative approach that involves creating realistic device emulations in a virtualized environment, allowing suppliers to conduct comprehensive functionality and security tests on emulated hardware. Our method allows for the customization of these emulations to match specific device types, facilitating the end-to-end testing of applications. We have validated our approach by implementing it in a cross-platform IoT development project, with our findings indicating that our emulations provide an effective and efficient means of testing IoT applications.

Recent findings from the LHCb collaboration have been presented to the LHCb Upgrade Proposal Review Panel, centered on the upgrades planned for the LHCb detector as it readies for Run 3 and beyond at the upgraded High Luminosity LHC. These upgrade proposals aim to significantly enhance the detector's performance, including a new forward telemetry system, a refined trigger and data acquisition setup, an improved vertex detector, and a new drift chamber. Such enhancements will allow the detector to manage the increased data rate resulting from the increased luminosity, while also facilitating significant upgrades to the software framework for a more efficient reconstruction of particles and better performance of analyses. Given its role in understanding the asymmetry between matter and antimatter, the LHCb experiment has a special focus on the rare and rarely occurring $B_s^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, a decay that the new detector will be able to produce 100 million times more often than the current setup, allowing the experiment to thoroughly investigate various $muon$-related aspects and fully $muon$ system calibration. Given its ability to calibrate the $muon$ system, the new detector will be able to achieve the highest precision ever recorded for $CP$ violation measurements in $B_s^0$ mesons and potentially discover the system-level asymmetries that could help explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. The development of autonomous driving systems heavily relies on robust artificial intelligence algorithms, which in turn require the extensive data sets that algorithms process. Generating high-quality traffic scenarios through artificial means is an essential step towards creating such datasets. We introduce a cutting-edge method for traffic scene synthesis, employing a traffic-structured variational auto-encoder (TS-VAE) model trained on real-world driving data. The TS-VAE learns the underlying statistical patterns of traffic scenes, incorporating both the spatial arrangement of vehicles and their individual attributes. Our model employs a multi-level encoding system, utilizing graphs to capture complex traffic relationships. It incorporates a attention-based decoder to focus on relevant parts of the graph when reconstructing the scene. Furthermore, we develop an efficient method for controlling the generator to produce samples aligned with given conditions. Our traffic scene synthesis method demonstrates superior performance in both unconditional and conditional applications, yielding highly authentic and diverse results in comparison to existing techniques.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

A vast array of existing methods are available for resolving time-dependent partial differential equations, and researchers continue to develop new solutions for their specific applications. When designing a scheme, fundamental properties must be taken into account such as stability, conservation, and the ability to capture high-frequency oscillations. A key consideration in developing numerical methods is ensuring a scheme can accurately represent long-term behavior, and researchers are exploring the use of artificial viscosity to achieve this. The paper provides a concise overview of current research on time-dependent PDEs, and in doing so, it can inform the creation of new artificial viscosity schemes.

A group of integer sequences can be classified as jointly ergodic if for every ergodic system with a measure-preserving nature, their average values, determined by iteratively applying the sequences, converge on average to a specific integral. We have developed finite obstruction theories for multi-sequence ergodic convergence, and this analysis has led to the discovery of ergodic convergence patterns that rely on non-uniformity in the original measure. This finding also indicates that traditional, uniform convergence theories for a single sequence, previously found by Bergelson and Friesen, and Bergelson and Hindman, are currently the most comprehensive.

We have developed a comprehensive model of superbubble evolution in low-metallicity environments, taking into account a range of factors, including a varying range of grain sizes in the supernova-affected region. During the early stage of superbubble evolution, we found that dust grains grow at a rate of approximately 0.01 micrometers per million years, provided that there is a sufficient supply of gas-phase silicon. As the superbubble expands and moves beyond this initial phase, the destruction rate of dust grains increases significantly, with a rate of about 0.003 to 0.025 micrometers per million years, depending on the age of the superbubble and its velocity. Consequently, the dust grain growth rate is only able to balance the destruction rate when the gas inflow rate exceeds approximately 0.01 solar masses per million years. This balance is unlikely to be achieved in most cases, as the rate of gas inflow is typically lower than this value. Therefore, we found that dust destruction rates are higher in environments where there are more massive and older stellar populations, as well as in regions where the dust grain supply is more abundant.

In autonomous vehicle navigation, detecting distant objects in the far-field is critical yet challenging with lidar sensors. A common approach involves using a convex hull to identify the far-field region based on points returned from the lidar. However, this method relies heavily on dense point cloud data, which is not always available in practice. As a result, boundary points within the far-field region may be missed, leading to inaccurate detection. To mitigate this issue, this paper proposes a new method for identifying the far-field that does not depend on a convex hull and can operate effectively even with sparse lidar data. The proposed approach uses a multi-layer perceptron to identify a binary classification for each point in the point cloud, based on a set of input features. These features include the 3D position and orientation of the normal vector in the local coordinate system of each point, as well as the 2D position of the projection of the normal vector on the image plane from a camera. To further enhance the method's performance, a far-field refinement step is added to remove incorrectly detected outlying points. The proposed approach has been tested and compared to the convex hull-based approach in simulated and real-world scenarios.

Chemical reactions are comprehensively described by a system's potential energy surface, which can be represented as a multidimensional landscape. The concept of a reaction path is analogous to a trajectory through this surface, often approximated using gradient flow. However, this approximation is limited to slow movements and neglects quantum effects. Our research explores the exact quantum dynamics of a system governed by the full cubic Hamiltonian, focusing on its time-dependent behavior. We analyze the time evolution of various quantities, such as position and momentum expectations, as well as correlations, for both coherent states and localized wave packets. By leveraging the symmetry of the Hamiltonian, we reveal the underlying structure of the potential energy surface, which informs our understanding of the reaction path and its connection to scattering dynamics. Notably, we find that the dynamics can be divided into two components: a time-periodic part associated with the 'classically trapped state' and a time-linear part linked to radiation or 'emitted state'. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that these components result from the interference of multiple classical trajectories.

Soft-tissue patient-specific device mapping is a non-rigid registration task, 
which is crucial for image-guided surgery. If we can transform a known device 
model into a post-deformation MRI scan of the device within a patient, we can 
determine its position and orientation in space. Due to its complex and variable 
nature, this type of transformation does not necessarily represent a physical 
deformation. To address this challenge, we propose utilizing an implicit 
deformable model that minimally assumes neighboring points in a structure maintain 
their relative positions. Although this model has been successfully used for 
various registration problems, its application to endoscopic surgery is unique. 
We present two strategies to solve the corresponding registration problem using 
this model. The first involves an iterative approach that refines the implicit 
representation to match an target shape. The second method employs a closed-form 
solution in conjunction with a sparse grid of control points. Our experimental 
results, obtained from MRI scans and physical models of surgical devices, 
demonstrate that our proposed methods perform comparably to state-of-the-art 
alternatives.

For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations.

Obtaining a dynamic 3D scene's depth map is heavily influenced by the accuracy of motion vectors. Accurate flow estimation not only provides the scene's motion information but also enhances the structure and occlusion details. In this paper, we present a novel method that simultaneously estimates motion vectors and depth maps for video sequences. Our approach, based on Bidirectional Single Stochastic Manifold, simultaneously models single-view motion and depth, as well as their interrelationship. Introducing additional terms for inter-media correlation, motion vector accuracy is improved, resulting in more precise depth map estimation. Notably, our method does not require training and delivers competitive performance compared to existing methods. Experimental results demonstrate the method's efficacy in handling real-world video sequences.

In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks have emerged as a low-power alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks, mimicking biological neurons and allowing time-varying computations. While this biologically-inspired approach has gained significant interest, a comprehensive analysis of its computational benefits over standard neural networks has yet to be conducted. To fill this gap, we performed a detailed examination of multiple Spiking Neural Network implementations on various architectures, performing the same tasks as their non-temporal counterparts. By evaluating them at the implementation level, we assessed the potential of these networks to deliver low-power computing. The results of this study provide the first detailed insights into the performance characteristics of Spiking Neural Networks, offering a foundation for further research and exploration.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that every perfect matching can be integrated into at least one Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first explored by Chvatal and Erdos in 1972. Our research focuses on identifying a variation, termed the PMH-property (PMH-property), where instead of requiring all perfect matchings to belong to the union of B-hypercomponents in a power of the graph, only a subset with maximum degree 2 is needed. Building upon a previous finding by Li and Liu in 2021, we prove a more general theorem: for connected, p-cyclic graphs with high connectivity and sufficient order, they possess the PMH-property. Specifically, we show that (2k+1)-regular, 2-k-cyclic graphs with connectivity and order also exhibit the PMH-property.

Recent discoveries in non-commutative algebraic geometry reveal that the Bunyakovsky Conjecture from number theory is equivalent to a specific statement made by Gelfand and Raikov in 1938. This statement asserts that certain types of sequences of functions, consisting of non-negative values, cannot uniformly approximate the constant function equal to one on the interval from zero to infinity.

This paper introduces a new system called Timeloops, an advanced filter that
identifies vulnerable system calls within microservices applications. In contrast
to static analysis-based techniques that often suffer from high false positives,
Timeloops leverages dynamic instrumentation and a predefined service map to
accurately determine the system calls a particular service is capable of executing.
Our experiments demonstrate that Timeloops outperforms existing dynamic
security baselines by significantly reducing false positives while maintaining
the ability to detect genuine security threats with 100% precision. Furthermore,
we show that Timeloops can automatically detect malicious system calls made by
various types of security-bypassing and -evading techniques employed by
microservices applications.

To address the issue of minimal Standard Model neutrino masses, the addition of right-handed neutrinos is necessary. These particles enable a neutrino mass generation mechanism, primarily through the Seesaw Type-I model. However, this assumption is difficult to confirm experimentally due to the challenge in producing heavy neutrinos at current particle colliders. Consequently, alternative neutrino mass generation mechanisms have been proposed within extended Standard Model frameworks that modify neutrino interactions by introducing new gauge forces. In this study, we investigate a specific model that combines an $U(1)_{B-L}$ extension with a triplet scalar field, and we develop a comprehensive set of evolution equations for all scalar fields and right-handed neutrinos, considering both perturbative scalar sector modifications and possible instabilities in the potential. We present evolution diagram representations of the model and utilize a numerical code to analyze the model's development, based on an assumed set of input parameters.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter is proposed to calculate the state posterior, assuming constant target velocities and known distributions. Unlike conventional PMBM filters utilizing Gaussian mixture models for target states, our approach models states with a grid-based intensity, significantly reducing computational costs. A state space reduction technique is also presented to efficiently manage large grids by concentrating resources on areas with higher density. Simulation results validate the method's accuracy and efficiency gains.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

The dynamics of soccer games mean that actions taken by a team in pivotal moments can significantly impact the match outcome. With limited data available, the action with the highest benefit isn't always apparent. This study introduces a new approach that accounts for the uncertain effects of an action on the score, based on historical performance of similar situations. This method integrates the benefits of different actions, which can be used to make optimal decision in real-time during the game. We demonstrate that this approach can find the best in-game actions and that executing these benefits can increase a team's chances of scoring. Additionally, we show that our model can assist coaches in making decisions, such as substituting players, to enhance the team's performance and lead advantage.

High-resolution subsurface imaging is typically achieved through wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI), an advanced variant of full waveform inversion.  In contrast to the original FWI formulation, WRI utilizes a non-linear objective function and starts from rough initial models, posing significant mathematical challenges.  This study formulates an adaptive optimization approach for WRI that leverages adaptive finite differences to adaptively modify the discretization of both model and data spaces.  This new method, called adaptive wavefield reconstruction inversion, translates the WRI problem into a sequence ofFWI sub-problems that can be resolved with established and efficient solvers.  Our formulation guarantees convergence to a stationary model under specific conditions, and we have incorporated it into the pytorch-based pypirom code. Through numerical simulations, we have demonstrated the accuracy of our approach through numerical experiments.

We have developed an innovative method to achieve optical nonreciprocity in Oam modes within solid-state resonators using Oam-selective photon feedback. Our approach utilizes quantum nondegenerate squeezing in resonator modes, combined with the quantum measurement and photon feedback techniques. Our theoretical model shows that optical nonreciprocity can be attained with lower requirements for nonlinearity and asymmetry compared to previous methods. Moreover, our scheme is compatible with existing Oam-selective photon feedback systems based on spatial light modulators. As a result, our proposal has potential applications in all-optical nonreciprocal devices and all-Oam isolators suitable for quantum communication and photonic integrated circuits.

We have analyzed the data from the Chandra HESSI and XMM-Newton to gain insights into the X-ray properties and spectral characteristics of the pulsar associated with the source IGR J19294+1816. Our observations have confirmed the spin cycle of the pulsar at 448.9 seconds and its spectrum can be effectively described by an absorbed thermal plasma model. Our results indicate the presence of a outflowing gas at 150 kilometers per second and a spin cycle consistent with that of the binary system. Our findings suggest the neutron star in this system is gaining angular momentum likely due to the transfer of momentum from the surrounding accretion disk.

The existing research into this topic often relies on abstract frameworks that generalize habitats into identical patches, which limits its applicability. Ancient sundials have been crucial for timekeeping and orientation throughout history. In classical Islamic civilization, the Sun's daily movement not only facilitated prayer direction but also helped synchronize religious rituals with the times of day. However, the fall of the Baghdad House of Wisdom and subsequent restrictions on scientific inquiry hindered the development of sophisticated sundials and caused existing ones to become obsolete. We have now recreated and improved upon historical sundials using 3D printing technology, allowing for accurate time measurement and direction finding. By utilizing modern additive manufacturing methods, we have created functional sundials that can be used in various settings, from personal devices to architectural installations. Our study demonstrates the benefits of 3D printing in restoring and enhancing timekeeping and navigational tools, opening up new possibilities for the application of sundials in contemporary society.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, combining D2D communication with DC. In this system, a DC transmitter sends signals to a D2D user while also providing energy to an energy-harvesting user, enabling data exchange between the two. We develop an optimal power allocation method to maximize the sum rate of D2D communication, considering the rate and power needs of the links, as well as the energy harvest from the DC transmitter. We analyze two scenarios, one where the DC and D2D transmitters are separate, and another where they are combined, and design power allocation policies for each. Finally, we demonstrate the benefits of integrating D2D communication with DC through numerical results.

The surge in telework and online learning due to the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the value of 2D LV technology for remote analysis of user reactions to interfaces and designs. By combining open-source LV and visualization software, researchers can efficiently evaluate the difficulty of navigating web pages and applications from a distance. A custom software package was created to automatically generate heat maps from LV data, reducing manual data processing and saving researchers significant time. This package can be easily integrated with popular data analysis tools like MATLAB and Python, streamlining the analysis process.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates (PEPPS) is examined, specifically their capability to compensate for spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). By doing so, PEPPS can enable a TEM to achieve a resolution as low as 0.05 \AA at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The compensation process involves the spherical phase plate mimicking a defocus effect. This defocus can be counterbalanced with a corresponding shift in the electron beam, resulting in a damped oscillation pattern in the spatial frequency domain. To address this issue, a PEPPS design is proposed that emulates the desired defocused aberration while maintaining a compact central aperture. The aperture's dimensions are around 0.2 \AA in radius, occupying approximately 14% of the total phase plate area. The aperture's impact on signal-to-noise ratio is minimal, accounting for less than 5% loss of incident electrons. The design's feasibility is validated through a detailed numerical calculation of the aperture's equivalent electrostatic geometry.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to effectively encode dialogue history for predicting suitable responses. This research investigates how various encoding techniques influence the effectiveness of predicting appropriate dialogue replies. By systematically altering the encoding methods and histories in our experiments, we use a set of fact-based test items to measure the changes in prediction accuracy resulting from different encoding strategies. Our findings reveal significant variations in the outcomes, indicating that certain encoding methods and histories lead to more accurate predictions than others. Moreover, we observe notable disparities in the performance of mainstream co-occurrence-based encoding techniques, underscoring their inability to consistently and reliably encode dialogue histories. These insights into the factors influencing prediction accuracy can guide the development of more effective encoding strategies for predicting suitable dialogue responses.

Deep learning is highly effective for LiDAR 3D place recognition and is now a key feature in modern autonomous vehicles. This research introduces a novel, computationally efficient LiDAR 3D place recognition approach that employs a deep learning network to classify locations. By utilizing a set of 3D interest operators and a subsequent deep learning network, the proposed method achieves high place recognition accuracy. Specifically, a light field correlator operator is introduced to extract local 3D descriptor features from LiDAR data, providing robust and geometrically meaningful place representations. These features are then used to train a deep learning network, which efficiently maps LiDAR data to a location classification output. Our approach exhibits superior performance compared to existing LiDAR 3place recognition methods across a variety of outdoor datasets.

Streaming high-quality video at resolutions above HD requires video transcoding,
which can be resource-intensive and is often facilitated by cloud computing.
Cloud transcoding employs multiple virtual machines (VMs) to process video,
but the number of required VMs depends heavily on the VM specifications.
Determining the optimal number and type of VMs for a cloud transcoding service
is a complex problem due to the wide variety of available VM options.
This study proposes a mixed integer linear programming model to address this
problem while taking into account the transcoding capabilities of each VM type,
the cloud service's fixed costs, and the processing capabilities of each VM.
A clustering algorithm is also developed to efficiently solve larger instances
of this problem. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed clustering
algorithm produces high-quality solutions closely matching optimal outcomes.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. This work introduces a new system for creating high-quality speech from written text, considering contextual elements. By incorporating sequential and semantic features, our system outperforms existing methods in preserving pronunciation and meaning.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies typically assume a single complex scalar field with a specific type of 'wrong sign cubic term' in its potential. Under these conditions, the potential can have an extremely high number of local minima and unstable states. We propose an energy barrier that prevents this issue, allowing for a 'cored Q-ball' that is potentially stable and can exist in various complex scalar field multiminima landscapes. Our model demonstrates the feasibility of cored Q-balls and can be applied to the electroweak phase transition through the interplay between the Higgs field and a new complex scalar field. In this application, the cored Q-ball is stable at high energies but becomes unstable after the phase transition, potentially solving the strong CP problem and providing a suitable dark matter candidate in the form of inert domain walls surrounding the Q-ball.

We investigated a cyclic universe containing holographic dark energy with different infrared cutoffs, excluding the Big Rip singularity. The study reveals that, in the absence of interaction between the cosmos sectors and the quantum correction to gravity, the HDE model based on the Hubble radius cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant within a cyclic universe framework. Furthermore, we discovered that the interaction between the dark sectors and the gravitational correction cause the HDE density to gradually decline over the course of multiple cycles, ultimately leading to a HDE density that is insufficient to halt the contraction of the universe before it transitions from its most compact state to the Big Bang.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a Hermitian matrix, for which an alternative proof has been devised, employing a method related to the zeta function of a graph. Furthermore, the formula has been broadened to cover regular coverings of graphs, and a novel 'L-function' concept has been defined for graphs. Additionally, an explicit expression has been derived for this L-function in a specific case, and the initial properties of the generalized Gnutzmann-Smith zeta function have been identified.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G.

The Belle II experiment at the KEKB collider can conduct in-depth searches for rare decays involving axion-like particles (ALPs). These particles, which interact very weakly with standard model particles, can be identified through multiple processes. One process of interest is the decay $B^+ \to K^+ \phi_i$, in which a $B$ meson decays into a $K$ meson and an ALP that subsequently decays invisibly. Due to the missing energy carried away by the ALP, this search requires precise measurements of beam momentum and vertex resolution. Using a dataset consisting of 0.502 $bb$ events from Belle II test data, we refined our understanding of $B^+ \to K^+ \phi_i$ signal reconstruction even with coarse-momentum measurements. With a full Belle II dataset of 50 $ab^{-1}$, this $B$-factory will be capable of exploring a broad ALP parameter space through $B$ meson decays for the first time or with significantly enhanced sensitivity compared to other methods.

This research paper examines the detection of diachronic semantic change in language using contextualized embeddings. While successful in capturing synchronic changes, our results suggest that extracting models of diachronic change from these embeddings is challenging due to their limited training data and inability to capture rare word senses. To address this issue, we propose using explicit sentence-level labels and massive corpora to enhance the detection of diachronic change, particularly for rare words. Our experiments show that these improvements can be achieved with relatively minor increases in model size.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are thought to be powered by a supermassive black hole that is actively consuming matter. The process of accretion is often accompanied by an accretion disk that emits X-rays. These X-rays can provide a wealth of information about the characteristics of the AGN, including the mass and spin of the black hole itself. To extract this information from the X-ray spectra, researchers need to account for how the X-rays are distorted as they escape from the accretion disk. In this study, we use numerical simulations to create distorted X-ray spectra for a specific type of AGN, one that has a disk that extends to the innermost stable orbit, a stable thick disk, and a relativistic outflow. We apply different levels of blurring to the spectra, ranging from the standard (Monorot) to the extreme (extreme GRADY), and we generate synthetic X-ray spectra for these four disk models. To make the process of analyzing AGN spectra more efficient, we also provide pre-computed templates that can be used in spectral fitting. Furthermore, we explore the effects of using these relativistic templates on the interpretation of observed AGN spectra. Our results show that the choice of disk model can have a significant impact on the inferred characteristics of the AGN, and that the use of extreme blurring can lead to an overestimation of the spin of the black hole. To address this issue, we propose a method

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic movement of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neural epithelium during interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). Through live imaging and statistical analysis, our research has developed a method to quantify IKNM rates by measuring the distance between a migrating nucleus and the upper surface of the neural epithelium. This quantitative approach was applied to monitor nuclear migration in the dorsal hindbrain of zebrafish. We have created an open-source package that can calculate IKNM rates and visualize results using genome-scale live imaging data. This tool facilitates the assessment of IKNM dynamics across large datasets, enabling researchers to identify patterns and anomalies in real-time. By providing a framework for quantitative analysis, our package can be utilized to study the effects of genetic mutations, chemical treatments, and physical injuries on the timing and coordination of cell processes during development.

In various image processing tasks, such as video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images are often observed through linear sampling masks, resulting in missing data. Recent studies have demonstrated that exploiting the horizontal and vertical code patterns present in these sampling masks can significantly enhance reconstruction performance. However, existing approaches have not fully capitalized on the code patterns' key characteristics: sparsity, scattered distribution, and absence in certain rows or columns. As a result, their reconstruction capabilities are limited. To overcome this challenge, a novel optimization model is proposed, taking these code pattern traits into account. To facilitate real-time implementation, a streamlined version of the proposed model is also developed. A comparison of simulations and experiments with state-of-the-art methods validates the superior reconstruction performance achieved by our approach.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

Researchers within the same institution frequently exchange information through email, instant messaging, and shared file systems. This study develops a risk assessment model for these institutions' communication networks, based on a comprehensive database of software vulnerabilities. Using this model, we analyze software vulnerability patterns in a representative sample of research institutions' computer networks. By applying a second-stage analysis and a meso-scale approach, we analyze the software vulnerability distribution across these networks. Our findings, simulated on a comprehensive database of nearly 10 million software instances, reveal that a significant majority (99.99%) of nodes within these networks are vulnerable to exploitation, with the most vulnerable 0.01% of nodes posing a substantial security threat. We also explore the concept of "super-spreader" nodes, which could facilitate the spread of malware within these networks. Our results indicate that the probability of such nodes existing is high (99.99%), and their prevalence could have a major impact on the overall software vulnerability landscape of these computer networks.

Inspired by recent experimental and theoretical work on strongly interacting electron systems, a new concept, the "exceptional" or "E-type" van Hove singularity, is defined in terms of the topological structure of the Fermi surface. This definition of an E-type singularity reveals limitations in the applicability of the Gutzwiller approximation and highlights the emergence of a complex, multi-sheeted branch point in the non-interacting Green's function. Close to an E-type singularity, the system displays characteristic behaviors, such as a local extremum in the Mott gap and a specific power-law relationship between the chemical potential and the interaction strength. A model of the square lattice Hubbard model with nearest-neighbor repulsion demonstrates the presence of an E-type singularity at $V_{nn}=4t$, resulting in a multi-sheeted branch-point in the lower bound of energies. Furthermore, a numerical study using the Continuous Time Quantum Monte Carlo method confirms that the Hubbard model exhibits an exceptional van Hove singularity under the same conditions.

This paper discusses the challenges of detecting spallation neutrons that result from cosmic-ray muons interacting with protons in a water tank. A specialized apparatus was set up at the Brookhaven National Laboratory to observe this phenomenon, taking advantage of the intense flow of neutrons available there. The setup included three layers of scintillator detectors arranged in a specific pattern to identify the initial muons and any resulting spallation neutrons. A significant increase in neutron detection rates was found when comparing areas with high and low neutron flux, providing a direct measure of the relative difference in neutron availability. Furthermore, an estimated 90% of the observed events were determined to be caused by neutrons, according to a detailed simulation of the process.

Ground-based observations of planetary systems are crucial in complementing the data from space-based missions like TESS and Kepler. Specifically, ground-based data help to measure the planetary masses and refine the understanding of planetary system architectures. A key application of these observations is the search for exoplanets within our own solar system's vicinity. A set of high-precision, existing velocity data was utilized in this study to identify potential exoplanets within the TESS field of view through a grid-based search. The results from this grid-based approach were compared to existing data and the outcomes of a more targeted follow-up to a TESS sector. Furthermore, a set of criteria for selecting optimal targets for ground-based verification of TESS candidates was established.
